varieties.name: Gold Dust (D. surculosa)
varieties.note: Not a cane dracaena at all: a shrubby West African understory plant with thin bamboo-like stems and oval leaves flecked cream and gold. It takes the least light of this group and scorches in a bright window, and it is slow enough that a season with no new leaf is not a complaint. Spots fade toward plain green in a dark corner.

varieties.name: Madagascar dragon tree (D. marginata)
varieties.note: Thin arching canes with narrow red-edged leaves. Wants the brightest light in this profile's range and drops its lowest leaves steadily as a matter of habit, not of health.

varieties.name: Corn plant (D. fragrans)
varieties.note: Thick canes and wide strappy leaves, often with a pale central stripe. The most forgiving of a dim room and the quickest to show tip burn from tap water.

varieties.name: Janet Craig (D. fragrans 'Janet Craig')
varieties.note: Plain dark green and glossy. Every leaf is working, so it holds up in lower light than the variegated kinds.

varieties.name: Lemon Lime (D. fragrans 'Lemon Lime')
varieties.note: Bright chartreuse edges on green. More variegation means less leaf doing the work: slower, and it wants the brighter end of the range to keep its colour.

varieties.name: Song of India (D. reflexa)
varieties.note: Short whorled leaves edged in cream on a branching stem. Resents cold draughts more than the rest and sulks after a move.

watering.label: Let the top third dry, and water with something other than hard tap water if the tips brown

drainage.label: Free-draining mix. These rot from the roots up long before they look thirsty

young: Too dark for a young plant. A rooted cutting has nothing in reserve and simply stops.
Dim. The stem stretches between leaves and the spots come through pale.
A little short for a young plant. It will hold the leaves it has and add none.
established: Too dark. The stems run bare and the plant leans toward whatever light there is.
Dim. Cream flecking fades toward plain green, which is the first thing to go.
A little short. It holds, but it will not put out a new stem.

young: Too much for a young plant. The newest leaves pale and their flecks wash out.
Well past what a young plant takes. New leaves crisp at the edge as they open.
Far too much for a young plant. Thin new leaves bleach and dry out within an afternoon.
established: Burning. The pale flecks go papery first, then dry to tan patches that do not recover.
Too much. Leaves bleach to a washed-out yellow and crisp at the edges.
Far too much. These grow under a canopy; a bare window burns them through.
